Slowly, his heart a frantic drum against his ribs, he closed the library door, the well oiled latch clicking home with a sound no louder than a sigh. For a moment he stood utterly still, listening to the ponderous silence of the great house; a silence broken only by the doleful ticking of a grandfather clock in the hall, each tick a leaden drop into the vast pool of the night. This was a fool's errand, an act of sheerest desperation, and he knew it. He, Julian Croft, who had never so much as pocketed a stray coin, was now a common housebreaker. The thought sent a hot wave of shame across his face.

With a shake of his head, he forced himself to move, his soft soled shoes making no whisper on the thick Persian rug. A sliver of moonlight, filtering through the tall arched window, was his only guide. It fell upon the monstrous, claw footed desk that dominated the room, its polished surface gleaming like a sheet of black ice. All around it loomed the implements of its owner's life: morocco bound legal texts, stacked in severe, intimidating columns; a bronze bust of some grim faced Roman senator; a humidor of dark, fragrant cedar; an array of silver framed photographs whose subjects all wore the same hard, proprietary stare. It was a room wholly without warmth, a chamber built for calculation and conquest; exactly the sort of room Ambrose Thorne would inhabit.

He had but one objective. The ledger. The slim, green leather volume in which Thorne recorded his most private, and most ruinous, transactions. And it must be here. With a deep breath that did little to steady him, Julian approached the desk, his fingers tracing its cold, carved edge. The main drawer was, as he had feared, locked fast. Why had he imagined it would be otherwise? Thorne was a man who locked everything: his gates, his doors, his heart. He drew from his pocket a thin, flexible palette knife, its steel a glint of wickedness in the gloom. To stoop to this; to pry and jemmy like a common thief! It was an ignoble business, altogether. What would Eleanor think, if she could see him now? The thought was a fresh torment, but it also steeled his resolve. For her, he would do this; for her, he would descend into this mire.

He worked the blade into the seam, feeling for the bolt. The wood groaned in protest. He applied more pressure, his knuckles white, his teeth clenched until his jaw ached. There was a sudden, sharp crack; a splintering sound that seemed to echo like a gunshot in the stillness. He froze, listening, but the house remained quiet. The drawer slid open. His hands, trembling now, fumbled through neat stacks of papers, through contracts and deeds, until they found it: a small book, bound in green leather, with no title upon its cover. He had it. A giddy, terrible sense of triumph washed over him.

Clang! The sound of the wrought iron gate swinging shut in the drive below sent a jolt of pure ice through his veins. He stood paralyzed, the ledger clutched in his hand. Headlights swept across the library window, painting the walls in a fleeting, ghostly yellow, and were gone. A car door slammed. Then another. Voices, one a familiar, booming baritone, the other a lighter, deferential murmur, drifted up from the gravel path. Thorne. He was home. A week early.

Panic, stark and absolute, seized him. There was no time to replace the ledger, no time to even close the drawer. His only thought was to escape notice, to melt into the very shadows he occupied. Across the room, heavy portieres of deep crimson velvet flanked the bay window, their folds offering the only conceivable sanctuary. Snatching up the ledger, he fled toward them, his careful silence abandoned in a mad, scrambling rush. The voices were in the hall now, the sound of a key in the main lock grating horribly on his nerves. He slipped behind the curtain an instant before the library door was thrown open, flooding the room with brilliant light from the hall. Huddled in the dark, smelling the dusty wool of the drapery, he held his breath.

"See to the fire, Jennings," came Thorne's voice, cold and clear as winter air. "And bring the brandy. We have matters to discuss before the morning."

A sliver of the room was visible through a gap in the fabric. Julian watched, a prisoner in his velvet cell, as the servant crossed to the hearth. He dared not move, dared not even breathe, as the man knelt to his task, his back not ten feet from Julian's hiding place. It was a trap. A damnable, hopeless trap.

The space behind the portiere was stifling, thick with the scent of aged wool and dust motes that tickled his throat, demanding a cough he dared not utter. He pressed the stiff, leather-bound ledger against his chest, its sharp corners digging into his ribs, a constant, painful reminder of his folly and his prize. The fire caught. The heavy sash resisted for a moment, then, with a low groan that was mercifully lost in the confusion, it began to slide upward.

The drop was farther than he expected, a good ten feet onto a manicured lawn, soft from a recent shower. He landed badly, his ankle twisting under him with a searing bolt of pain. A cry was torn from his throat, but he bit it back, his teeth sinking into his lip until he tasted blood. He lay stunned on the wet grass for a precious second, the dark, imposing mass of the house looming over him. Above, the library window was a rectangle of warm, damning light. He had to move.

Scrambling to his feet, ignoring the fire in his ankle, he began to run. He limped grotesquely, half-stumbling, across the vast, dark lawn, heading for the distant shadows of the tree line that bordered the property. Every step was agony. He did not look back. He did not dare. He ran on, fueled by terror and a wild, desperate triumph. He was out. He was free.
